clue.text: Copper rod cut by the worker in Hickey's gag

indicators.note: cut means the rod word is docked, losing its final letter

parts.note: a rod is a pole
Hickey, the salesman in O'Neill's The Iceman Cometh, jokes that his wife is off with the iceman, the man who delivers ice

explanation.surface: A police officer's truncheon gets interrupted by a tradesman from a stage salesman's running joke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut' trims POLE to POL; 'by' simply sets the iceman beside it. Hickey is the salesman in Eugene O'Neill's play The Iceman Cometh.
explanation.definitionFit: Copper is informal British slang for a police officer.

clue.text: Scott's Cavalier hero's threat about English verse

indicators.note: about means the threat word goes round the other letters

parts.note: a threat or danger is a peril

explanation.surface: A swashbuckling Royalist from Walter Scott menaces the English poetry scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts EV inside PERIL, after its first letter. Walter Scott's novel Peveril of the Peak has a Cavalier hero.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Walter Scott named his Restoration novel after its Royalist protagonist, Julian Peveril.

clue.text: Climbing beast's no new monster

indicators.note: in a down clue climbing means the letters are read upwards, so backwards
no means the letter for new is left out of the beast word

parts.note: a beast is an animal

explanation.surface: A creature scaling a wall turns out to be no fresh horror.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no' removes N from ANIMAL to leave AIMAL, and 'Climbing' turns that upwards into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Lamia was a child-devouring she-demon, later a serpent-woman, as in Keats's poem.

clue.text: Is the monarch unable to conceal tale-tellers' aim?

parts.note: asking whether the monarch is unable is asking: can't ER?, with ER the Queen's royal cipher
to conceal something is to bury it

explanation.surface: A question about whether the sovereign cannot keep something secret.
explanation.walkthrough: The question 'Is the monarch unable?' is rephrased as CAN'T ER (ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the monarch). Chaucer's pilgrims tell their tales on the road to Canterbury.
explanation.definitionFit: Chaucer's storytelling pilgrims were journeying to Becket's shrine in that Kentish cathedral city, their destination.

clue.text: University withperiodicals about Maurice Conchis?

indicators.note: about means the periodicals word goes around the university letter

parts.note: the clue runs 'with' and 'periodicals' together; periodicals are magazines, informally mags, and 'with' only links

explanation.surface: A college with its journals is asked about a character from a novel.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue as published runs 'with' and 'periodicals' together. Maurice Conchis is the enigmatic magician figure in John Fowles's novel The Magus.
explanation.definitionFit: Conchis is the title character of Fowles's novel, the sorcerer who stages illusions on a Greek island.

clue.text: Food that's posh eaten by Tintin, or as a dog's breakfast

indicators.note: eaten by means the posh letter is swallowed inside the jumbled letters
a dog's breakfast is a British idiom for a total mess, so the letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: U is the old label for upper-class or posh usage

explanation.surface: Tintin's dog Snowy gets a meal described as either posh or a complete mess.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as a dog's breakfast' (British for a mess) is the anagram signal and 'eaten by' the container. U means posh from the old U and non-U labels; Tintin's dog Snowy makes the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Nutrition is nourishment, the food a body takes in.

clue.text: A Boojum mocking criticism

definitions.meaning: in Lewis Carroll's The Hunting of the ..., the creature hunted proves to be a Boojum, a dangerous kind of the beast
sarcastic, snide comment is called this in modern slang

explanation.surface: A Carroll monster that delivers sarcastic put-downs.
explanation.definitionFit: Carroll's poem says 'the Snark was a Boojum', and the word is also slang for sarcasm.

clue.text: The fourth chap put on heroin

parts.note: to put something is to set it
H is slang for heroin

explanation.surface: A fourth man is placed on hard drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: After Adam, Cain and Abel, Adam's son Seth is the fourth man named in Genesis.
explanation.definitionFit: In Genesis this son of Adam is the fourth male person to appear, after his father and two brothers.

clue.text: Playful article set in a novel location

parts.note: arch means playfully mischievous
an is the indefinite article
to gel is to set, as a jelly does

explanation.surface: A mischievous piece of writing is placed in a book's setting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' only links. Archangel, the northern Russian port, is the location and title of Robert Harris's thriller.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Harris's novel takes its title from the Russian port city where much of it is set.

clue.text: Kant primarily behind promoting North German writer

indicators.note: primarily means only the first letter of the philosopher's name is used
promoting moves the letter for north up to an earlier place in the word

parts.note: astern means behind, at the back of a ship

explanation.surface: With Kant as the main backer, a northern German author is championed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'promoting' lifts the N one place earlier in the behind word; 'primarily' takes K from Kant. Erich Kästner wrote Emil and the Detectives.
explanation.definitionFit: Erich Kästner was a German novelist and poet, author of Emil and the Detectives.

clue.text: Very famous Kipling book initially lacking energy

indicators.note: initially lacking means the book title loses its first letter

parts.note: Kim is Rudyard Kipling's novel of an orphan in India

explanation.surface: A celebrated Kipling novel is said to start without much vigour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially lacking' drops K from KIM to leave IM.
explanation.definitionFit: Vim is vigour or liveliness, a colloquial word for energy.

clue.text: US clubs close before TLS leader stays

parts.note: nigh means near or close

indicators.note: leader means only the first letter of the paper's initials is used

parts.note: to stick is to stay put

explanation.surface: Something nearly happens before the editor of the paper remains in place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'before' only links the pieces in order.
explanation.definitionFit: American police carry these batons, also called billy clubs or truncheons.

clue.text: Edgar Wallace's sleuth reported with craft for his audience?

indicators.note: reported means the detective's name is used for how it sounds when said

parts.note: Mr J. G. Reeder is the mild-mannered detective in Edgar Wallace's stories
a craft is a boat or ship

explanation.surface: A crime writer's detective is mentioned along with a boat meant for his public.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the definition as describing the people who read Wallace.
explanation.definitionFit: An author's audience is the body of people who read him, his public.

clue.text: Writer of some German novels

indicators.note: some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: An author of several German novels.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Mann wrote German novels such as Buddenbrooks, so the surface is literally true.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Mann was a German novelist, the author of The Magic Mountain.

clue.text: Preserve low fees, upsetting the Hero of Quebec

parts.note: jam is a fruit preserve

indicators.note: upsetting means the letters of the two words are overturned and rearranged

explanation.surface: A complaint that keeping fees low upsets a famous general.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upsetting' rearranges LOW FEES into ESWOLFE. General James Wolfe died taking Quebec in 1759.
explanation.definitionFit: General Wolfe died winning the 1759 battle on the Plains of Abraham, which took the city for Britain.

clue.text: Cryptically, I role play

parts.note: these letters are built by the wordplay the answer describes: a look word (LO) turned back, sitting inside a word for anger (IRE)

explanation.surface: A cryptic hint that the speaker is acting a part.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: read the answer as instructions. LO, looked back, is OL; put it in IRE (anger) and you get I ROLE. John Osborne's 1956 play is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: John Osborne's 1956 drama started the Angry Young Men movement in British theatre.

clue.text: Decorates books in gold stars

parts.note: or is gold in heraldry

indicators.note: in means the books letters are placed inside the stars word

parts.note: stars or celebrities are big names
NT is the New Testament, a set of books

explanation.surface: Someone adorns volumes among golden stars.
explanation.walkthrough: OR is the heraldic word for gold.
explanation.definitionFit: To ornament something is to adorn or embellish it.

clue.text: Poet's ecstasy amid mountain features

indicators.note: amid means the drug letter sits in the middle of the mountain words

parts.note: a col and a ridge are both features of mountain terrain
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: A poet's rapture among the peaks, apt for a Lake District writer.
explanation.walkthrough: One phrase, 'mountain features', supplies two words, a pass and a ridge, and 'amid' puts E between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Samuel Taylor Coleridge was a Romantic poet, author of The Rime of the Ancient Mariner.

clue.text: Left popular capital after amusing time making a spy film

indicators.note: after means the left, popular and capital pieces follow the amusing time pieces

parts.note: something amusing is fun
an era is a period of time
in means fashionable or popular
Berlin is the capital of Germany

explanation.surface: A trendy capital is left behind after good times, the making of a thriller.
explanation.walkthrough: Len Deighton's novel, filmed with Michael Caine as Harry Palmer in 1966.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1966 Cold War espionage movie starring Michael Caine was adapted from Len Deighton's novel.

clue.text: Tiny mark leads to exam resits for Hassan's author

parts.note: a fleck is a small spot or mark

indicators.note: leads to means the first letters of the two following words are used

explanation.surface: A small blemish leads to a student retaking exams.
explanation.walkthrough: James Elroy Flecker wrote the verse drama Hassan.
explanation.definitionFit: James Elroy Flecker wrote the verse play Hassan, staged in 1923 after his death.

clue.text: Strange tutor — and not about to add learners!

parts.note: nor means and not
re means about or concerning
L is a learner, so two Ls are learners

explanation.surface: An odd teacher who refuses to take on more students.
explanation.walkthrough: In Susanna Clarke's Jonathan Strange and Mr Norrell, Norrell is Strange's tutor in magic. L for learner comes from British L-plates.
explanation.definitionFit: In Susanna Clarke's novel the magician Norrell takes Jonathan Strange as his pupil.

clue.text: Line taken from introductory theme for Madame Bovary?

indicators.note: taken from means the line letter is removed from the theme word

parts.note: a lemma is a preliminary proposition, or a heading giving the theme of a passage

explanation.surface: A line is lifted from the opening theme of Flaubert's novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Madame Bovary's first name is Emma; the question mark flags definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Flaubert's heroine is Emma Bovary, so the first name fits her as an example.

clue.text: A poet's advice to avert a hangover

definitions.meaning: John ... was an English poet and dramatist
taking fluids is the usual tip for avoiding the morning-after misery

explanation.surface: A poet's tip for not feeling rough the next morning.
explanation.definitionFit: John Drinkwater was a Georgian poet; downing a glass of fluid is the standard hangover precaution.

clue.text: "Now cracks a — heart. Good night, sweet prince .. (Hamlet)

definitions.text: "Now cracks a — heart. Good night, sweet prince .. (Hamlet)

parts.words: "Now cracks a — heart. Good night, sweet prince .. (Hamlet)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank from Horatio's farewell to the dying prince at the end of Hamlet

explanation.surface: Horatio's lament over Hamlet's death.
explanation.definitionFit: Horatio's farewell line praises Hamlet's heart as high-minded and honourable.

clue.text: Nell, so called Little Flower

definitions.meaning: Dickens's Little Nell in The Old Curiosity Shop has this surname
a flower is something that flows, a crossword term for a river, here the English Midlands river

explanation.surface: A girl named Nell is nicknamed Little Flower.
explanation.definitionFit: Little Nell's full name is Nell Trent; the Trent is a major English river, a flower in crossword terms.

clue.text: One shot supporting a schemer

indicators.note: in a down clue supporting puts the shot word underneath the a

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
a shot is a go or attempt

explanation.surface: Someone is shot while backing a plotter.
explanation.walkthrough: Iago is the scheming villain of Othello.
explanation.definitionFit: Iago is Shakespeare's arch-plotter in Othello, a byword for treachery.

clue.text: King with a banal need, reordering a bestseller

indicators.note: reordering means the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A king with a dull need rewrites a popular book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reordering' turns BANAL NEED into NEANDABEL. Jeffrey Archer's Kane and Abel is the bestseller.
explanation.definitionFit: Jeffrey Archer's 1979 saga sold millions of copies worldwide.

clue.text: The first mate envies every other character

indicators.note: every other character means alternate letters of the next word are taken

explanation.surface: The original spouse is jealous of everyone else.
explanation.walkthrough: Eve, Adam's wife, was the first mate in Genesis.
explanation.definitionFit: In Genesis Adam's wife was the first woman, the first partner of a man.

clue.text: Richard, originally American, like this Pulitzer winner

indicators.note: originally means only the opening letter of the name is used

parts.note: so means like this, in this way

explanation.surface: Richard, born an American, is a prizewinning writer of this kind.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard Russo won the 2002 Pulitzer Prize for fiction for Empire Falls, so 'Richard' fits the surface as well as the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Russo won the 2002 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction for Empire Falls.

clue.text: For Lorca the European lament, strangely primitive

parts.note: Lorca wrote in Spanish, where 'the' is el

indicators.note: strangely means the letters of the word are rearranged

explanation.surface: A Spanish poet's European lament sounds oddly primitive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strangely' turns LAMENT into MENTAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Elemental means basic, fundamental, primal.
